---
title: "Tabular foundation models"
---

This vignette is a **theory-first** digest of Christoph Molnar's
open book
[*Tabular Foundation Models*](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/introduction)
(2026). The original has twelve chapters; here we keep the
definitions, the PFN story, and one concrete Python family per
applied task. We do not re-run Molnar's benchmarks.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope

Molnar's "Understanding" part is built around
`nanoTabPFN` (educational). He sets aside hypernetworks, cross-table
transfer, and **LLM-over-tables**. This course chapter follows that
restriction.
:::

## Why tables were late to foundation models {#sec-tfm-why}

A **table** is a matrix of rows (instances of one entity) and columns
(features of that entity). Inside one table the types mix: text,
integers, dates, missingness. Between tables the *shape* mixes: two
columns of timestamps versus thousands of gene-expression columns.

For images, a pixel is a pixel. For language, a token is a token. For
tables, two columns named `sales_fruit_banana` and `id_12319_ban` may
or may not mean the same thing. Shuffling rows or columns should not
change the scientific object, but it *does* change what a naive
transformer sees. That is why tabular ML stayed with
**gradient-boosted trees** while vision and language consolidated on
pretrained transformers ([Vaswani et al., 2017](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/7181-attention-is-all-you-need)).

A **foundation model** is a large model pretrained on a vast corpus
and reused across tasks. A **tabular foundation model (TFM)** is
pretrained to solve *predictive* tasks on tables.

## Prior-data fitted networks {#sec-pfn}

[Prior-data fitted networks](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/prior-data-fitted-networks)
(PFNs; [Müller et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2112.10510))
raise the unit of learning from a **row** to a **task**: a table split
into train and test, with one target column.

| Classical ML | PFN-based TFM |
|--------------|----------------|
| Train weights on one dataset | Pretrain on millions of (usually synthetic) tasks |
| Expensive `fit`, cheap `predict` | Cheap `fit` (load weights), expensive in-context `predict` |
| Hyperparameter search per table | The "search" was done in pretraining |

**In-context learning** here means: the model adapts to a new table
*without updating parameters*. The training matrix is part of the
forward pass.

Molnar's preferred PFN-style TFMs share four traits:

- transformer with row- and column-wise attention;
- PFN training objective;
- pretraining mostly on synthetic data (structural causal models are
  a common prior);
- prediction by in-context learning.

Families in the wild (names from Molnar's introduction, not an
exhaustive census): TabPFN (Prior Labs;
[Hollmann et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2207.01848)),
TabICL (Inria), TabDPT, SAP-RPT-1-OSS, Seldon, Nexus, TabFM, EXAONE-Tabular.

### Bayesian reading {#sec-ppd}

Let $D=(X_{\mathrm{train}},y_{\mathrm{train}})$ and let $x_*$ be a new
row. The object of interest is the posterior predictive

$$
p(y\mid x_*, D)
= \int p(y\mid x_*,\phi)\,p(\phi\mid D)\,d\phi,
$$

where $\phi$ indexes latent supervised tasks. Expanding with Bayes'
rule makes the **task prior** $p(\phi)$ explicit: pretraining is
approximate Bayesian inference over that prior. At test time the
network returns an approximation to $p(y\mid x_*, D)$, not a single
tree.

## Applying TFMs (one example per task) {#sec-apply}

Syntax looks like `scikit-learn`. Do not be fooled: `.predict(X_test)`
still consumes the training table in the background.

Chunks below are **not** evaluated at render time. Install
`tabicl` locally if you want to reproduce Molnar's labs
(`tabicl==2.2.0` in his classification chapter).

### Classification {#sec-tfm-clf}

[Chapter 6](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/classification) uses
**TabICL** (`TabICLClassifier`) on a small multi-class UCI problem
(land-mine type from three sensors). `.fit` downloads weights and
encodes columns; `.predict_proba` is the slow step. On that example
Molnar reports TabICL beating a heavily tuned `XGBoost` classifier.
Levers when `predict` is too slow: fewer ensemble members, GPU, KV
cache, fewer features (attention is quadratic in the number of
columns).

```python
# Sketch only — see Molnar, ch. 6
from tabicl import TabICLClassifier

clf = TabICLClassifier(random_state=1)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_hat = clf.predict(X_test)
```

**TabPFN** is the historically first PFN classifier for *small*
tables (seconds, not a long GBM search). Use it when $n$ is modest
and you want a calibrated predictive distribution out of the box.

### Regression {#sec-tfm-reg}

[Chapter 7](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/regression) keeps
the same in-context story with a **different pretraining head**.
The running example is **TabICL** (`TabICLRegressor`) on UCI wine
quality: predict a continuous score from physicochemical columns.
Default prediction is the mean of the predictive distribution;
`output_type="median"` switches to the median.

Molnar compares default TabICL with a `RandomizedSearchCV`-tuned
`CatBoostRegressor` on a 25% hold-out and reports lower MAE/RMSE
and higher $R^2$ for TabICL *on that split*. That is an illustration,
not a universal ranking.

TabICL regression is itself an **ensemble** (default eight members).
Diversity comes from feature order (circular shifts, permutations)
and optional Yeo–Johnson transforms — a patch for attention treating
identically scaled columns as interchangeable. `n_estimators` trades
accuracy for wall-clock time; on the wine example, one estimator was
almost as accurate as eight.

```python
# Sketch only — see Molnar, ch. 7
from tabicl import TabICLRegressor

reg = TabICLRegressor(random_state=1, n_estimators=8)
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_mean = reg.predict(X_test)
y_median = reg.predict(X_test, output_type="median")
```

### Quantile regression {#sec-tfm-qreg}

[Chapter 8](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/quantile-regression)
uses the same wine table. TabICL regression is pretrained to emit
**999 quantiles**; `output_type="quantiles"` plus `alphas` picks a
subset (for example $0.1$, $0.5$, $0.9$). Mean prediction is
implemented by aggregating those quantiles. Extra $\alpha$ levels are
essentially free at `predict` time.

A 10%--90% band is a prediction interval, not a confidence interval
for a mean. Molnar reports pinball loss per $\alpha$ and empirical
coverage of the 80% band close to nominal on that hold-out. That is
the TFM analogue of a GBM trained with pinball loss, without a
separate quantile model.

### Time series {#sec-tfm-ts}

[Chapter 9](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/forecasting)
turns forecasting into regression: `TabICLForecaster` wraps
`TabICLRegressor`, adds calendar / cyclic features from timestamps,
and attends to a context window (Molnar notes a 4096-row cap). There
is no extra RNN. Dedicated models such as TimePFN exist when you want
a prior that was *pretrained* on synthetic series rather than a
wrapper. Equidistant grids without gaps are required if you ask the
wrapper to roll a `prediction_length` forward.

## Betting on the stack {#sec-outlook}

Molnar's last part argues that TFMs may inherit the **LLM stack**
(pretrain once, adapt in context, ship as an API) rather than remain
one more exhibit in the tabular zoo. For this course the practical
takeaway is narrower:

- On **small-to-medium** rectangular problems, try a TFM before a
  long GBM search.
- Keep trees when you need cheap batch prediction, strict
  feature-budget latency, or an audit trail of splits.
- Never treat a TFM chart from ChatGPT Images as a substitute for
  `predict` on *your* held-out rows.

Further reading starts at
[tabularfoundationmodels.com/introduction](https://tabularfoundationmodels.com/introduction).
